Hard times

Heartbreak

A break-up or unrequited love can hurt like a physical wound. What happens in the mind and what helps you move on.

Being left, leaving someone you still love or falling for someone who does not love you back are almost universal experiences. And yet those going through them usually feel that no one has ever suffered so much.

It really hurts

In neuroimaging studies, looking at a photo of an ex-partner who has just left activates brain regions related to reward and craving, similar to those involved in addiction, and also some involved in pain. This helps explain the urge to know about the other person, check their social media or write to them again, even when one knows it is not wise.

The two sides of unrequited love

Roy Baumeister and colleagues collected accounts from people who had loved without being loved back and from people who had turned someone down. Both sides suffered. The lover felt pain and humiliation, but also hope; the rejecter felt guilt and did not know how to say no without hurting. Remembering that rejection is not always a judgement on one's worth helps stop it becoming a bigger wound.

When to worry

Intense distress usually lasts weeks or a few months and gradually eases, with ups and downs. It is worth seeking help if months go by without improvement, if you stop eating or sleeping, if thoughts of not wanting to live appear, or if you turn to alcohol to cope. Break-ups are one of the most common triggers of crises in adolescents and young adults.

What tends to help

  • Reducing contact and reminders. Unfollowing the other person and putting their things away for a while helps the craving fade.
  • Rebuilding your own identity. Long relationships mix hobbies and friendships; recovering or creating your own helps you feel like yourself again.
  • Making sense of what happened without blaming yourself for everything: understanding what went wrong and what you have learned.
  • Leaning on friends and accepting invitations even when you do not feel like it.
  • Looking after the basics: sleep, food, movement. It seems little, but it sustains mood.

References

  1. Fisher, H. E., Brown, L. L., Aron, A., Strong, G. y Mashek, D. (2010). Reward, addiction, and emotion regulation systems associated with rejection in love. Journal of Neurophysiology, 104(1), 51–60.
  2. Baumeister, R. F., Wotman, S. R. y Stillwell, A. M. (1993). Unrequited love: on heartbreak, anger, guilt, scriptlessness, and humiliation. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 64(3), 377–394.
  3. Slotter, E. B., Gardner, W. L. y Finkel, E. J. (2010). Who am I without you? The influence of romantic breakup on the self-concept. Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin, 36(2), 147–160.
